title: Not every repeat deserves a skill
caption: A skill written too early locks in a procedure nobody has proven.

alt.scene: The control room. The pilot, the AI model, sits at the console beside a fat ring binder bursting with thin card tabs, several red. A long skill index spills off the page; several entries are stamped never tested, and the one you need is buried seventh.

skills-written-too-early.header: Skills written too early: Knuth on premature optimisation
skills-written-too-early.description: "We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil. Yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3%" [1]. His reason is a cost, and the same paper calls ignoring efficiency in the small "an overreaction", so it is a rule about timing and measurement. The quotes were not checked against the original (the ACM page returned 403).

knuth-structured-programming.title: Knuth, Structured Programming with go to Statements

skills-nobody-needs-yet.header: Skills nobody needs yet: YAGNI, and what it does not cover
skills-nobody-needs-yet.description: "Always implement things when you actually need them, never when you just foresee that you need them" [1]. Fowler counts four costs of a presumptive feature (build, delay, carry, repair) and says YAGNI does not apply to effort to make software easier to modify [2].

jeffries-yagni.title: Jeffries, You're NOT gonna need it!

a-crowded-skill-index.header: A crowded skill index costs the AI too
a-crowded-skill-index.description: by default every skill's description is loaded on every turn, unless the skill is user-only, and Claude Code and Codex cap or shorten the skill listing, so a crowded index can shorten or drop descriptions [1][2].

anthropic-claude-code-skills.title: Anthropic, Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code docs)

too-early.title: Too early
too-early.script: Now the opposite danger. If you write the skill after the first run, you freeze a guess, and a procedure nobody has proven now carries the authority of a skill.

a-thin-card-has-a-price.title: A thin card has a price
a-thin-card-has-a-price.script: And every quick skill has a price. It is one more thing to keep right and one more line in an index that only grows, so picture a manual stuffed with thin cards, several of them never tested, until the one you need is buried in the middle.

three-questions.title: Three questions
three-questions.script: So before you write a skill, ask three questions. Does the task repeat, does it have rules, and does a mistake cost something? If the answer is no to all three, leave it in the chat. This check is mine, a practical filter I use, not a published test.
